question: According to the Connecticut CDL manual, what is the single most important reason for inspecting your commercial vehicle?
choice_a: To maintain the vehicle's resale value
choice_b: To avoid receiving a traffic citation
choice_c: Safety, for yourself and for other road users
choice_d: To satisfy the motor carrier's insurance paperwork
explanation: The manual states that safety is the most important reason you inspect your vehicle, both for yourself and for other road users.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-1

question: What is the minimum tread depth required in every major groove on the front tires of a commercial vehicle?
choice_a: 8/32 inch
choice_b: 2/32 inch
choice_c: 4/32 inch
choice_d: 6/32 inch
explanation: The manual requires at least 4/32-inch tread depth in every major groove on front tires, versus 2/32 inch on other tires.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-1

question: On a 20-inch steering wheel, roughly how much rim movement (steering wheel play) is enough to make the vehicle hard to steer?
choice_a: Any play at all, even less than 1 degree
choice_b: Play of more than 10 degrees, about 2 inches of rim movement
choice_c: Play of more than 25 degrees, about 5 inches of rim movement
choice_d: Play of more than 45 degrees, about 9 inches of rim movement
explanation: The manual notes steering wheel play of more than 10 degrees, approximately 2 inches of movement at the rim of a 20-inch steering wheel, can make it hard to steer.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-2

question: During a suspension inspection, what fraction of missing or broken leaves in a leaf spring puts the vehicle 'out of service'?
choice_a: One-fourth or more
choice_b: Three-fourths or more
choice_c: Any single missing leaf
choice_d: One-half or more
explanation: The manual states that if one-fourth or more of the leaves in a leaf spring are missing, the vehicle will be put out of service, though any such defect can be dangerous.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-2

question: Which combination of warning devices satisfies the required emergency equipment for a parked commercial vehicle?
choice_a: Three reflective triangles, or at least 6 fuses, or 3 liquid-burning flares
choice_b: A single liquid-burning flare and a first aid kit
choice_c: One reflective triangle and a flashlight
choice_d: Two fuses and a fire extinguisher only
explanation: Required warning devices for parked vehicles are three reflective triangles, or at least 6 fuses, or 3 liquid-burning flares.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-3

question: During the in-cab inspection, within what time frame should air pressure build from 50 to 90 psi?
choice_a: Within 10 minutes
choice_b: Within 30 seconds
choice_c: Within 3 minutes
choice_d: Within 1 minute
explanation: The manual states air pressure should build from 50 to 90 psi within 3 minutes, continuing to the governor cut-out pressure.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-4

question: When starting the engine on a vehicle equipped with Anti-lock Braking System (ABS), what should the ABS indicator light do?
choice_a: Come on and then turn off
choice_b: Never illuminate under normal conditions
choice_c: Stay on continuously for the entire trip
choice_d: Flash red until the vehicle reaches highway speed
explanation: The dash ABS light should come on and then turn off; if it stays on, the ABS is not working properly.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-4

question: To test a hydraulic brake system for leaks during the seven-step inspection method, what should you do?
choice_a: Apply the parking brake and pull forward gently against it
choice_b: Pump the brake pedal three times, then apply firm pressure and hold it for five seconds; the pedal should not move
choice_c: Hold the brake pedal down for 30 seconds without pumping first
choice_d: Pump the brake pedal once and release it immediately
explanation: For hydraulic brakes, the manual says to pump the pedal three times, then apply firm pressure and hold for five seconds; if the pedal moves, there may be a leak.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-7

question: Why does the manual recommend backing and turning toward the driver's side whenever possible?
choice_a: It is faster than backing toward the right side
choice_b: It is a legal requirement in Connecticut
choice_c: It reduces wear on the right-side tires
choice_d: It allows the driver to see better by looking out the side window
explanation: Backing toward the driver's side lets the driver watch the rear of the vehicle by looking out the side window; backing toward the right is dangerous because the driver can't see as well.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-8

question: When using a helper while backing, what should the driver and helper agree on before backing begins?
choice_a: The exact speed of the vehicle in miles per hour
choice_b: A set of hand signals, including a signal for 'stop'
choice_c: Which mirror the helper will stand near
choice_d: The route the vehicle will take afterward
explanation: The manual advises working out a set of hand signals with the helper before backing, including agreeing on a signal for 'stop.'
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-8

question: Which type of manual transmission requires double clutching to change gears?
choice_a: Automatic transmissions with a manual shift mode
choice_b: Synchronized manual transmissions
choice_c: Any transmission with more than five forward gears
choice_d: Unsynchronized manual transmissions
explanation: Most heavy vehicles with unsynchronized manual transmissions require double clutching; if equipped with a synchronized manual transmission, double clutching is not required.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-9

question: When can mirror adjustment on a combination vehicle be checked most accurately?
choice_a: While making a sharp turn
choice_b: Prior to the start of any trip, when the trailer(s) are straight
choice_c: Only after the vehicle has been driven for an hour
choice_d: Only at night using headlight reflections
explanation: Mirror adjustment should be checked prior to the start of any trip and can only be checked accurately when the trailer(s) are straight.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-10

question: According to the manual, how far ahead should most good drivers look while driving?
choice_a: Only as far as the vehicle immediately in front
choice_b: 30 to 45 seconds ahead
choice_c: 12 to 15 seconds ahead
choice_d: 3 to 5 seconds ahead
explanation: The manual states most good drivers look at least 12 to 15 seconds ahead, which is about a quarter mile at highway speeds.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-10

question: How do objects appear in a convex ('fisheye,' 'spot,' or 'bug-eye') mirror compared to looking at them directly?
choice_a: Larger and closer than they really are
choice_b: Smaller and farther away than they really are
choice_c: The exact same size and distance
choice_d: Upside down and reversed
explanation: The manual explains that everything appears smaller in a convex mirror than it would if you were looking at it directly, and things seem farther away than they really are.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-11

question: Which of the following is one of the manual's rules for using turn signals?
choice_a: Signal only after you have already begun turning
choice_b: Signal well before you turn so others don't try to pass you
choice_c: Use the horn instead of a signal in heavy traffic
choice_d: Only signal for turns, never for lane changes
explanation: The manual's first rule for turn signals is to signal early, well before you turn, as the best way to keep others from trying to pass you.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-11

question: If you must stop on or by a one-way or divided highway, where should you place your warning devices?
choice_a: 5 feet, 50 feet, and 100 feet in a line behind the vehicle
choice_b: 25 feet on each side of the vehicle
choice_c: 10 feet, 100 feet, and 200 feet toward the approaching traffic
choice_d: Only directly behind the rear bumper
explanation: On a one-way or divided highway, warning devices should be placed 10 feet, 100 feet, and 200 feet toward the approaching traffic.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-12

question: Which three distances add up to a vehicle's total stopping distance?
choice_a: Acceleration distance, cruising distance, and coasting distance
choice_b: Perception distance, reaction distance, and braking distance
choice_c: Following distance, passing distance, and turning distance
choice_d: Sight distance, signal distance, and skid distance
explanation: The manual defines total stopping distance as perception distance plus reaction distance plus braking distance.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-13

topic: Effect of Speed on Stopping Distance
question: If you double your speed from 20 mph to 40 mph, what happens to your vehicle's braking distance?
choice_a: It stays the same
choice_b: It becomes about 4 times longer
choice_c: It becomes about 9 times longer
choice_d: It doubles
explanation: The manual states that doubling speed from 20 to 40 mph makes the impact and braking distance about 4 times greater.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-14

question: Why do empty trucks often require greater stopping distances than fully loaded trucks?
choice_a: An empty vehicle has less traction
choice_b: Empty trucks always have smaller tires
choice_c: Empty trucks have weaker brakes installed at the factory
choice_d: Empty trucks are required by law to drive faster
explanation: The brakes, tires, springs, and shock absorbers on heavy vehicles are designed to work best when fully loaded, so empty trucks require greater stopping distances because they have less traction.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-14

question: What is 'black ice' as described in the manual?
choice_a: Ice that forms only on bridges
choice_b: A type of studded winter tire tread pattern
choice_c: A thin, clear layer of ice that makes the road look wet
choice_d: Ice mixed with road tar that turns the pavement black
explanation: Black ice is a thin layer that is clear enough to see the road underneath, making the road look wet; watch for it any time the temperature is below freezing and the road looks wet.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-14

question: According to the manual, hydroplaning can occur at speeds as low as what, if there is a lot of water on the road?
choice_a: 10 mph
choice_b: 30 mph
choice_c: 50 mph
choice_d: 65 mph
explanation: The manual states hydroplaning can occur at speeds as low as 30 mph if there is a lot of water on the road.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-14

question: Why does the manual say braking in a curve is dangerous?
choice_a: It is illegal to brake while turning the steering wheel
choice_b: It automatically triggers the ABS warning light
choice_c: It is easier to lock the wheels and cause a skid
choice_d: It causes excessive fuel consumption
explanation: The manual warns that braking in a curve is dangerous because it is easier to lock the wheels and cause a skid; drivers should slow to a safe speed before entering the curve instead.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-15

question: A driver operating a 40-foot vehicle at a speed under 40 mph should leave at least how much following distance, using the manual's rule of thumb?
choice_a: 4 seconds
choice_b: 1 second
choice_c: 8 seconds
choice_d: 10 seconds
explanation: The rule is at least one second of following distance for each 10 feet of vehicle length at speeds below 40 mph, which is 4 seconds for a 40-foot vehicle.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-16

question: If you are being tailgated, what does the manual advise against doing?
choice_a: Avoiding sudden changes in speed or direction
choice_b: Signaling early before slowing or turning
choice_c: Flashing your brake lights or taillights as a 'trick' to warn the tailgater off
choice_d: Increasing your following distance ahead of you
explanation: The manual specifically advises against tricks such as turning on your taillights or flashing your brake lights to discourage a tailgater; instead, increase following distance and avoid quick changes.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-17

question: Why might a cargo van that cleared a low bridge while loaded fail to clear that same bridge later?
choice_a: An empty van sits higher than a loaded one, reducing clearance
choice_b: Bridges settle lower every year
choice_c: Posted bridge heights are always measured for loaded vehicles
choice_d: Tire pressure has no effect on vehicle height
explanation: The weight of a cargo van changes its height; an empty van is higher than a loaded one, so clearing a bridge while loaded does not mean you can clear it while empty.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-18

question: How does the manual define a 'hazard'?
choice_a: Any vehicle traveling faster than the posted speed limit
choice_b: Any road condition or other road user that is a possible danger
choice_c: Only a situation that has already caused a collision
choice_d: A hazard exists only on wet or icy roads
explanation: The manual defines a hazard as any road condition or other road user, such as a driver, bicyclist, or pedestrian, that is a possible danger; seeing it early lets you prepare before it becomes an emergency.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-18

question: What do move-over laws generally require drivers to do when approaching a stopped emergency vehicle or roadside incident?
choice_a: Sound the horn continuously while passing
choice_b: Stop completely until the emergency vehicle leaves the scene
choice_c: Slow down and change lanes away from the emergency vehicle or incident when it is safe to do so
choice_d: Turn on high-beam headlights to alert workers
explanation: Move-over laws require drivers to slow and change lanes when approaching a roadside incident or emergency vehicle; if a lane change is unsafe, the driver should slow down and proceed with caution instead.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-19

question: Why does the manual identify rental trucks as a hazard clue related to blocked vision?
choice_a: Rental trucks are always overloaded
choice_b: Rental truck drivers are often unfamiliar with the limited side and rear vision the truck provides
choice_c: Rental trucks are exempt from vehicle inspection requirements
choice_d: Rental trucks are not equipped with mirrors
explanation: The manual notes rental trucks should be watched carefully because their drivers are often not used to the limited vision they have to the sides and rear of the truck.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-19

question: What does the 'slow moving vehicle' warning symbol described in the manual look like?
choice_a: A red triangle with an orange center
choice_b: A yellow diamond with a black exclamation point
choice_c: An orange square with red stripes
choice_d: A blue circle with a white arrow
explanation: The manual describes the slow moving vehicle symbol, used to warn of vehicles like mopeds, farm machinery, or construction equipment, as a red triangle with an orange center.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-20

question: Which of the following is listed as a clue that another driver may be impaired (sleepy, drunk, on drugs, or ill)?
choice_a: Maintaining a steady, consistent speed
choice_b: Weaving across the road or drifting from one side to another
choice_c: Keeping a safe following distance at all times
choice_d: Signaling every lane change well in advance
explanation: The manual lists weaving across the road or drifting from one side to another as a clue of an impaired driver, along with sudden speed changes and stopping at the wrong time.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-20

question: Under the federal rules referenced in the manual, what is the CDL disqualification period for a driver's second conviction within 3 years for hand-held mobile telephone use while operating a CMV?
choice_a: 30 days
choice_b: 180 days
choice_c: 120 days
choice_d: 60 days
explanation: A CDL is disqualified for 60 days for a second offense within 3 years, and 120 days for three or more offenses within 3 years, for hand-held mobile telephone use while operating a CMV.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-22

question: How much greater are the odds of a safety-critical event (crash, near-crash, or unintentional lane deviation) for CMV drivers who text while driving, compared to those who do not?
choice_a: 23.2 times greater
choice_b: 6 times greater
choice_c: 12 times greater
choice_d: 2 times greater
explanation: Research cited in the manual shows the odds of a safety-critical event are 23.2 times greater for CMV drivers who text while driving, making texting the most alarming distraction because it combines physical and mental distraction.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-22
